title: 6 Hard-hitting Truths that Every Leader Needs to Face
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Gaurav Jain argues that effective leadership requires accepting six uncomfortable truths, and that the sooner a leader embraces them the more effective they become. Each truth is anchored in an anecdote from his own management career: a manager blaming a low performer for a red project, his early people-pleasing habit of spreading bonuses evenly, a manager proud that her team had never had a conflict, and managers who shared engagement-survey action plans but never acted on them. The six truths are that accountability starts with the leader, that a leader's success depends on the team, that not everyone will like you, that conflict is inevitable, that leaders do not have all the answers, and that legacy is defined by actions rather than intentions. The piece offers practical rules alongside them, such as saying "we" when sharing success and "I" when owning failure, and actively mining for conflict by creating a safe environment to surface it. It closes by urging leaders to embrace these truths rather than resist them.
points: Blaming a team member for a delay reflects poorly on the manager, who is responsible for both the delivery and the performance of the team.
A concrete language rule: use "we" more than "I" when sharing accomplishments, and "I" more than "we" when taking accountability for failures.
Jain's early habit of "peanut butter spreading" bonuses to avoid upsetting anyone illustrates why trying to please everyone produces flawed decisions.
Telling a team that conflict is bad does not remove it but drives it underground; leaders should actively mine for conflict in a safe environment.
Managers who shared engagement-survey action plans but took no action saw the same issues return, showing that legacy rests on action, not intention.
quotes: What this manager didn’t realize was how poorly it was reflecting on him, as he was ultimately responsible for not just the project delivery, but also the performance of his team members. If there were poor performers on his team, why wasn’t this issue addressed earlier?

No matter how challenging the goals, or how unfavorable the circumstances may have been, you are accountable for the outcome. Blaming external factors or even team members for failures or setbacks will only reflect poorly on your leadership.
As a practice, you should use We more than I when you share stories of accomplishment. And use I more than We when you are taking accountability for failures.

However, I soon realized that it was impossible to please everyone, and the entire strategy I was trying to implement was flawed. As a leader, I needed to make the decision that was right for the organization. Period.

Just like a pigeon cannot make the approaching cat disappear by closing its eyes, a leader cannot make a conflict disappear by avoiding it. Doing so will only exacerbate the underlying issues, and make it harder to resolve them later.
As a leader, you don’t need to know the solutions to every problem thrown at you. You need to be okay with saying “I don’t know” and be willing to seek input from others to find the solution.

However, what I noticed was that most managers simply shared their action plans but failed to take concrete actions. This was evident as the same opportunities emerged repeatedly in the subsequent surveys.
